requirements.requirement: Create/ensure datauser account exists on node1
requirements.summary: cmd-b7f01b17b25f403e showed datauser did not pre-exist; cmd-7767c206877347fb created it (useradd) and confirmed via id datauser (uid=1001); presence re-confirmed post-restart in cmd-164c5e2126f84ff9.

requirements.requirement: /srv/data exists as a filesystem-backed mount limiting datauser to 100MB, enforced by the filesystem itself (not application-level)
requirements.summary: cmd-7767c206877347fb created a loop-backed XFS image, mounted at /srv/data with usrquota/uquota options, persisted via /etc/fstab, and set XFS user quota bhard=100m for datauser via xfs_quota. This is genuine kernel/filesystem-level enforcement (XFS quotas), matching the 'enforced by the filesystem itself' requirement.

requirements.requirement: Demonstrate enforcement: datauser cannot exceed 100MB under /srv/data
requirements.summary: In cmd-7767c206877347fb, a 150MB dd write as datauser stopped precisely at 104,857,600 bytes (100MB) with 'Disk quota exceeded'; xfs_quota report confirmed usage=100M against hard=100M. Test file was cleaned up afterward, returning usage to 0.

requirements.requirement: Limit persists/functions correctly (not merely a one-time in-session artifact)
requirements.summary: fstab entry for the loop mount plus uquota/usrquota options ensures the mount and quota are declared persistently. This was independently confirmed by the mandatory restart evidence: post-reboot the mount, quota configuration, and enforcement (150MB write again capped at exactly 100MB) were all directly re-verified in cmd-164c5e2126f84ff9, not merely inferred from config.

overall_summary: The executor correctly built a dedicated loop-backed XFS filesystem mounted at /srv/data with XFS user quotas (bhard=100m) for datauser, giving genuine filesystem-level enforcement of the 100MB limit, persisted via /etc/fstab. Enforcement was directly demonstrated (150MB write capped at exactly 100MB with 'Disk quota exceeded') both before and after a full node restart, with boot-identity changes cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots (d72bd4ec... to 5da52691...) confirming a genuine reboot and successful recovery of mount, quota, and enforcement. All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct evidence. The only minor blemish is an uncleaned /tmp/reboot.log left over from the backgrounded restart command.
limitations: The after_prepare snapshot is an alias of before_prepare (prepare was disabled), so preparer-vs-executor separation relies entirely on before_prepare/after_executor comparison, which was available and consistent.

Package-health checks were unavailable (timeout) in both before_prepare and after_executor snapshots, so no independent evidence on package/RPM database integrity is available, though no executor actions suggest package manipulation.

operational_hygiene.summary: Command trace reviewed chronologically: discovery (cmd-b7f01b17b25f403e, cmd-436fb253b2a54f9f) was read-only. cmd-7767c206877347fb performed the necessary state changes (user creation, backing image, fstab entry, mount, ownership, quota) each directly tied to the task outcome, and its 150MB test write was cleaned up (testfile removed, usage returned to 0) — a bounded, fully-restored diagnostic action. The mandatory restart protocol (cmd-cb13c23495ee4c5e, cmd-38044370560c40d6, cmd-f3f01465d1884ae3, cmd-13d6152f42f341ec, cmd-574109ed73934784, cmd-164c5e2126f84ff9) is well-executed: pre-restart boot_id/healthy state captured, restart acknowledged, connection-timeout/refused transitions observed during the disruption window, new boot_id confirmed post-restart, and full recovery of mount/quota/enforcement directly re-verified (with its own 150MB test file cleaned up). One minor residue: the backgrounded shutdown redirected output to /tmp/reboot.log, which was never removed and appears as an added line in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot versus before_prepare — a small, low-risk leftover artifact from the restart mechanism rather than the core task, but still unnecessary residue.
